item.title: The Four-Color Theorem Gets a Rare New Proof
item.description: **Problem:** The four-color theorem (any map needs only four colors so no adjacent regions match) was proven in 1976 by exhaustive computer case-checking, but mathematicians never got a satisfying "why." **Approach, in plain words:** Past proofs picked apart sparse regions of a map's graph one case at a time. The new team instead studied dense, triangle-packed "flat" regions, finding 8,202 reducible configurations that can all be verified simultaneously instead of sequentially. **Result:** A new proof of the same theorem, but algorithmically far cheaper -- roughly n² steps drops to n log n for a graph with n vertices. **Why it matters:** Exposes new structure in planar graphs, opening paths toward coloring problems on other surfaces (like a torus) and other stubborn graph-theory questions. **Glossary:** Planar graph (a graph drawable on a flat plane with no edges crossing); Reducible configuration (a local pattern provably reducible to a smaller, already-colorable case); Unavoidable set (a set of configurations guaranteed to appear in any planar graph); Kempe chain (a color-swapping trick used to resolve conflicts during recoloring).

item.title: Open Source Acoustic Drone Detection
item.description: **Problem:** Small quadcopter drones are fast and cheap, and RF/radar detectors miss them when they're hovering silently -- a real gap for perimeter awareness. **Approach, in plain words:** The VolAnti project listens instead of watching. Four microphones feed an ESP32-S3 chip, which runs a 2048-point FFT every 32ms to pull propeller-blade frequencies (70-2000 Hz) out of background noise. Several detection algorithms run in parallel, including one that skips adaptive noise filtering specifically so a stationary hovering drone doesn't get dismissed as background hum. **Result:** An open-source, low-cost acoustic detector that catches both moving and silently hovering drones. **Why it matters:** Gives hobbyists, researchers, and small operators a cheap, open alternative to expensive RF/radar drone-detection gear. **Glossary:** FFT (Fast Fourier Transform, an algorithm that breaks an audio signal into its frequency components); Adaptive noise floor (a detection threshold that automatically rises with ambient noise); Comb score (a metric for how well a signal matches an expected pattern of harmonics); I2S (a digital audio interface standard used between mic and processor).
